sections.heading: The idea
sections.body_md:
A **system** maps an input signal \(x(t)\) to an output \(y(t)\). Two properties make a system easy to analyse. It is **linear** if scaling and adding inputs scales and adds outputs: the response to \(a x_1 + b x_2\) is \(a y_1 + b y_2\). It is **time-invariant** if delaying the input only delays the output, with no change in shape. A system with both properties is **LTI**.

Many physical systems are LTI to a good approximation: a spring, mass and damper; a tank draining through a valve at small flows; a resistor-capacitor network; a motor driving a light load. They are described by linear differential equations with constant coefficients. Anything that clips, saturates, squares, or has parameters that change with time breaks the property.

The payoff is superposition. Once you know the response to one simple input, you can build the response to any input that is a sum of shifted, scaled copies of it. A quick test for nonlinearity is to double the input and see whether the output doubles. A quick test for time variation is to delay the input and see whether the output is only delayed. A system driven by a sinusoid that produces new frequencies cannot be LTI.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
\[ \mathcal{S}\{a x_1 + b x_2\} = a\,\mathcal{S}\{x_1\} + b\,\mathcal{S}\{x_2\} \]
\[ \mathcal{S}\{x(t - t_0)\} = y(t - t_0) \]
\[ a_n y^{(n)} + \dots + a_0 y = b_m x^{(m)} + \dots + b_0 x \quad (\text{constant } a_i, b_i) \]

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md: Test \(y(t) = 7x(t) + 0.4\). Doubling the input gives \(14x + 0.4\), not \(2(7x + 0.4) = 14x + 0.8\). The constant offset breaks linearity, even though the plot is a straight line. A system \(y(t) = t\,x(t)\) is linear, but a delayed input gives \(t\,x(t - t_0)\), not \((t - t_0)\,x(t - t_0)\). So it is time-varying.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md:
- Calling a straight-line input-output graph "linear" when it has an offset.
- Forgetting that a zero input must give a zero output in a linear system.
- Treating a system with a time-dependent coefficient as time-invariant.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Superposition lets you describe an LTI system by one response, to an impulse or to a complex exponential, and predict its output for any input. Convolution, transfer functions and Bode plots all rest on it.
